title: SDK repository conventions and sample layout
content:
Purpose
This doc establishes lightweight, developer-friendly repository conventions for Redwood SDKs and example repos. Goal is a predictable layout that makes onboarding fast, reduces cognitive load for maintainers, and standardizes release/CI expectations across languages and clients.

Audience
- SDK authors (internal and external)
- Solutions engineers publishing example apps
- Maintainers of language clients and adapters

Design principles (short)
- Minimal friction for getting started: zero-setup examples where possible.
- Consistent layout across languages so engineers can find auth, samples, and tests quickly.
- Small surface area for CI and publishing: one canonical path for build/test/release.
- Explicit boundaries between API surface, transport adapters, and samples.

High-level repo types and recommended defaults
1) Single-language SDK (recommended for core clients)
   - Use when the repo contains a single official SDK (js, python, go, java).
   - Root is package/module. Examples and tests live inside repo. Use semantic versioning and tags.
2) Polyglot repo (mono-repo for multiple SDKs)
   - Use if teams want a single CI and cross-language shared tooling (rare for community libs).
   - Require well-defined top-level folders (e.g., /clients/js, /clients/py, /clients/go).
3) Example / Starter app repo
   - Minimal dependency on SDK internals; depends on published packages or local workspace symlinks.

Canonical file layout (single-language SDK example)
/
  README.md                    -> short intro + one-liner quickstart (copy-paste)
  LICENSE
  .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE.md
  .github/workflows/ci.yaml    -> standardized CI (lint, unit, smoke, publish on tag)
  package.json / pyproject.toml / go.mod
  src/                         -> main client implementation (language idiomatic)
  lib/ or dist/                -> build output (ignored by default)
  examples/                    -> 1-3 minimal runnable examples (hermetic)
    /hello-world/              -> 30s demo using environment var API key
    /serverless/               -> example showing cold-start considerations
  tests/                       -> unit and integration tests
  e2e/                         -> optional end-to-end smoke scripts (CI gate)
  docs/                        -> extended docs, design notes, migration guides
  tools/                       -> helper scripts (dev server, local mock)
  CHANGELOG.md                 -> human-friendly release notes
  .npmignore / MANIFEST.in     -> packaging filters

Notes on README content
- 3 sections only: TLDR (one copyable example), Where to get help (issues/slack), How to run tests locally.
- Include a compatibility matrix (Redwood API versions and SDK versions).

Examples: what a "copy-paste" quickstart should look like (JS example)
- npm i @redwood/sdk
- export REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk_...
- node -e "const r = require('@redwood/sdk'); r.generate('Hello')"

API exports and surface area conventions
- Keep the public surface explicit: an index file that re-exports only stable items (no internal helpers).
- Avoid large default objects. Prefer named exports for clarity.
- Mark experimental features with an `experimental.` namespace and document stability.

Transport/adapters separation
- Transport code (http/websocket/edge-worker shims) must live under src/adapters/ or src/transports/.
- Core API code should depend on an abstract transport interface, not a concrete connector, to enable lightweight shims (e.g., deno, edge).

Examples directory guidance
- Each example must be hermetic: include a tiny package.json/pyproject pinned to local workspace or minimal dependency on published SDK.
- Include a simple smoke script: `yarn example:hello` or `python -m examples.hello` that runs with only an API key.
- Avoid long-running servers in examples; prefer short scripts that return an exit code.

Testing and CI
- CI must include: linting, unit tests, type checks (if applicable), and a lightweight e2e smoke that calls a Redwood test endpoint or the mock server from /tools/mock-server.
- Use a single matrix entry for minimum supported runtime (node 18, python 3.10, go 1.20). Additional matrix entries are optional.
- Secrets: do not store real keys in CI. Use ephemeral test tokens or Redwood Vault integration.

Release and versioning
- Semantic versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH).
- Release process: create a changelog entry (CHANGELOG.md) and tag the repo (vX.Y.Z). CI job publishes on a tag to the language registry.
- For monorepos: use a per-package version file and a release tool (changesets, lerna, or equivalent) to avoid accidental global bumps.

Dev ergonomics and local iteration
- `tools/devserver` or `tools/link-local` helper for linking an example to a local SDK build.
- Portable dev environment: prefer scripts over globally installed tools (e.g., `npm run dev` wraps `npx esbuild` etc.).

Packaging filters and small footprint
- Explicitly exclude heavy build artifacts and example data from packages. Provide a small published tarball (<200KB source) for faster installs in CI and demos.

Code samples style guide (short)
- Keep examples < 40 lines. Use top-level async/await. Provide explicit error handling for network calls. Clear comments for required env vars.

Onboarding checklist for a new SDK repo (two-minute checklist)
- [ ] README TLDR + copyable snippet present
- [ ] Example hello-world that runs with only API key
- [ ] CI: lint, unit, smoke e2e configured
- [ ] CHANGELOG.md exists and has initial entry
- [ ] License and Code of Conduct included
- [ ] Publish automation configured to run on tag

Maintenance notes and common gotchas
- Dont accidentally export secrets in example logs. Add a CI step that scans for `sk_` hardcoded tokens.
- Keep the dependency tree tiny: lock or pin dev deps in package files.
- When changing adapter interface, add a migration guide in docs/ and a compat test in e2e/.

Open items / TODOs
- Decide standard minimal example set (hello-world, serverless, streaming demo).
- Publish a canonical github template repo that implements this layout for each language.
- Add a small CLI helper `redwood-sdk-init` that bootstraps the layout and README.

Appendix: minimal CI recipe (GitHub Actions snippet description)
- Trigger: push + PR + tag
- Jobs: setup -> install -> lint -> test -> run smoke -> on tag: build -> publish
- On PR, skip publish; on tag push, publish artifacts to registry.

Why this matters
A consistent repo structure and small onboarding surface reduces support load for Solutions and DevRel by enabling customers and partners to run examples in minutes. It also speeds internal iteration when multiple teams implement language bindings or adapters.

If you want a follow-up, I can: generate a concrete repo template for JS/TS and Python, and a GH template repo with CI already wired up.
